Regress

rih-GRESS · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To regress is to go back to an earlier, worse condition.

Economists warned that the region's economy could regress to pre-pandemic unemployment levels if the factory closed.

Worked Example

Under extreme stress, the usually calm toddler began to regress, suddenly wanting a bottle again after months of drinking from a cup.

Regress means slipping backward to an earlier stage, not simply staying the same or getting slightly worse.

How Regress Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

backslide

backslide: to slip back into an earlier, worse habit or condition

deteriorate

deteriorate: to become progressively worse

Antonyms

advance

advance: to move forward or improve

progress

progress: to develop or improve over time

How Strong Is It? — stall → regress → collapse

stall vs. regress

stall vs. regress: To stall is simply to stop making progress, without necessarily going backward.

collapse vs. regress

collapse vs. regress: A collapse is a sudden, total breakdown, far more extreme than a gradual regression.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back (Latin)

root — gress

root — gress: to step, to walk (from Latin gradi, whose past stem is gress-)

Put it together

Put it together: Regress is built from re- ('back') + gress ('to step, to walk,' from Latin gradi, whose past stem is gress-) -- literally 'to step back,' which is exactly what happens when someone or something regresses to an earlier state.

Use the root in a new word: progress

Use the root in a new word: progress: The construction crew made steady progress on the new bridge despite the winter weather.
